analysis.one_liner: Requires periodic pressure testing and operator training for hazardous liquid pipelines to prevent spills.
analysis.headline: The pipeline safety bill never left committee: after hearings in 1989, it was never brought up for a vote and died when the Congress ended in January 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have directed the Secretary of Transportation to write rules requiring companies that run hazardous liquid pipelines to periodically verify the integrity of their pipes—either by hydrostatic pressure testing or by lowering operating pressures—and to test, within one year, older pipe made by a welding process linked to failures. It also would have required pipeline operators to be trained to recognize abnormal conditions that signal a dangerous situation, and ordered a study of leak detection technology. It was referred to two House committees and heard in subcommittees, but was never reported out or voted on.
analysis.who_benefits: People living near hazardous liquid pipelines, communities and waterways that would otherwise bear the cost of spills, and emergency responders. Hydrostatic testing finds weaknesses in old pipe before they cause ruptures, and operator training addresses human error during abnormal operating conditions.

how_it_helps.text: Requires operators to periodically assess the integrity of all hazardous liquid pipeline facilities through hydrostatic testing or other methods, or reduce maximum operating pressure to add a safety margin [S2] [S3].

Mandates testing within one year for pipeline made by the electric resistance weld process before April 1, 1970 that has never been hydrostatically tested—pipe of a type associated with seam failures [S2] [S3].
Changes operator training from optional to mandatory, including the ability to recognize and react to abnormal operating conditions that may indicate a dangerous situation such as a spill [S2] [S3].
Directs a study of advanced leak detection equipment and techniques, with recommendations to Congress within a year, laying groundwork for possible future requirements [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Pipeline operators—oil and hazardous liquids shippers—bear the cost of testing, pressure reductions, compliance schedules, and training. Some of that cost could be passed through to fuel and product prices, and untestable old pipe segments might have to be replaced or retired.

drawbacks.text: Hydrostatic testing and pressure reductions are costly, and compliance schedules set by regulation could force expensive repairs or retirement of older pipe segments, with some of the cost potentially passed to consumers through transport rates [S3].

A one-size mandate to assess all facilities, with only a one-year deadline for the oldest untested weld pipe, gives regulators limited flexibility to prioritize lines by risk, which critics of broad safety mandates commonly raise [S3].
Testing is disruptive: taking a pipeline out of service for hydrostatic tests can interrupt deliveries of fuel and other liquids to communities that depend on it [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The safety payoff is direct: old weld-seam pipe that has never been pressure tested is a known rupture risk, and testing or lower operating pressure addresses it before a spill, not after. The costs are real but targeted—testing, some pressure limits, and training—rather than an open-ended burden. On balance the bill's benefits to people living along pipelines and to waterways outweigh its compliance costs, though faster deadlines for the oldest pipe would have raised transition costs.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to two House committees and sent to their energy, power, and surface transportation subcommittees, which held hearings in 1989, but no committee ever voted to send it to the full House, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced May 18, 1989 by Rep. Ike Skelton, with one Democratic cosponsor, and referred jointly to the Energy and Commerce and Public Works and Transportation Committees [S1] [S4] [S5].
It was referred to the Energy and Power and Surface Transportation subcommittees in early June 1989 [S5].

Members held field hearings in Cambridge, Ohio; San Jose, California; and Denver, Colorado, and the subcommittees held hearings on July 12 and 13, 1989; the Department of Transportation and OMB were asked for their comments [S5].
After those hearings, no further action appears in the record—no markup, no committee report, no floor vote—through the end of the 101st Congress on January 3, 1991 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hazardous liquid pipeline operators avoided the mandated testing, pressure limits, and training costs; communities near pipelines did not get the protections, which Congress later addressed in pipeline safety legislation after more accidents.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Pipeline operators; the public did not get the protections

for.name: Rep. Ike Skelton
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and pressed it through two field hearings and subcommittee hearings in 1989.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Energy and Power Subcommittee but never reported it out or scheduled a markup.

against.name: House Public Works + Transportation Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Surface Transportation Subcommittee, which held hearings, but the committee never took it up for a vote.

sides.party_line_note: The record shows almost no contested action: the bill drew a single Democratic cosponsor and died in committee, with no votes from which to measure party positions.

industries.industry: Hazardous liquid pipeline operators (oil and petroleum products)
industries.note: The bill would have required periodic hydrostatic testing or lower operating pressures across their systems, plus mandatory operator training, at significant compliance cost. Their financial interest in avoiding these mandates ran against the safety interests of people living along the lines.

industries.industry: Petroleum and hazardous liquid shippers and refiners
industries.note: Testing and pressure limits could disrupt deliveries and add transport costs that partly pass into fuel prices. The bill's spill prevention benefit accrues to communities and waterways instead.
